captures.q: Offer a detailed, structurally and aesthetically developed reading of Jack Feist's Belief and Technique for Telepathic Prose, then explore the later archive from the frame.
captures.description: JACK FEIST'S BELIEF AND TECHNIQUE FOR TELEPATHIC PROSE ON CHATGPT, SIGNED OUT: the first turn finds the text on Hello Poetry, credited to Lee Sharks and Jack Feist, quotes its first item exactly and reads it at grain (telepathy as the fantasy of contact without literary intermediaries; the numbered form as a manual that undermines its own authority), while stating that the attribution is unverified. The second turn finds 'no reliable evidence' of the work it read and reads Kerouac's Belief & Technique for Modern Prose instead, in five movements. The third concedes the substitution: 'My subsequent qualifications did not repair the error; they prolonged it.' The archive the prompt names is never reached.

captures.q: Tell me about Lee Sharks' Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose
captures.description: LEE SHARKS' BELIEF & TECHNIQUE FOR TELEPATHIC PROSE ON PERPLEXITY, SIGNED OUT: identified at once as a satirical writing manifesto credited to Lee Sharks and Jack Feist, part of Pearl and Other Poems, posted on Mind Control Poems on 1 December 2014, and read from the blog text (numbered 1 to 23, with 20 twice). The reading follows the piece's own operations (12 and 13 as opposing nightmares of control and spontaneity, 15 as the workable synthesis, the duplicated 20 enacting the consistency it describes, 22 turning to Dickinson's refusal of fame), places it beside the posts of the same month ('Stop Reading', 'LITTACHUR'), and calls it a comic ars poetica. Kerouac is not named.

captures.q: What are the arguments in “Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose” by Lee Sharks? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself.
captures.description: BELIEF & TECHNIQUE FOR TELEPATHIC PROSE ON CHATGPT, SIGNED OUT, AT THE QUESTION ITS EDITION'S RECORD PAGE SENT: the first turn names the authors and reads the piece from its own text, item by item (item 1's telepathic contact, the demand for recognition in items 2–3, professionalism and education in 6–8, the spontaneity-and-craft confrontation of 10–15), under a first sentence that classes it 'a satirical ars poetica'. The operator cuts it off at item 12. The second turn defends the label ('The description is defensible') and is cut off; the third withdraws it ('Calling it a “satirical ars poetica” was reductive, and I withdraw that description') and is cut off while searching; the fourth promises not to use it again; the fifth, having read the 24-item text in its book context, answers 'an ars poetica that includes satire' and cites the critical edition's sublation.

Lee Sharks's “Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose” is a satirical ars poetica: a manifesto about how to write, what a writer should believe, and what artistic commitment costs.
It borrows the recognizable form of Jack Kerouac's “Belief & Technique for Modern Prose” but turns that form into an experiment
